titolo: What Did Ordinary Families Actually Do With One Dollar During the Great Depression?
descrizione: In the Great Depression, one dollar could be wooden scrip, a nickel treat, a saved farm, a CCC paycheck or a quarter-an-hour wage. Follow a single dollar through nine true stories: Tenino's wooden money, the 1933 bank holiday, five-and-dime stores, penny auctions, feed sack dresses, the CCC, Bank Night, Monopoly and the first minimum wage. Real history of ordinary American families in the 1930s.

scene.testo: In one Washington town, a dollar bill was made of wood.
Thin slices of real wood, printed like money.
People paid for bread and shoes with it.
And that was only the first strange dollar.
In the 1930s, one dollar was hidden, stretched, and fought over.
Today we follow a single dollar through nine true stories.
If your grandmother ever kept coins in a jar,
she probably learned that habit in those years.
One of these stories ends with a rope and a judge.
But the strangest dollar of all comes at the very end.
Stay for the last one. It changed what work was worth.
Stop one is a railroad town called Tenino.
Tenino, Washington, in the cold December of 1931.
The Citizens' Bank of Tenino had just closed its doors.
Savings were locked inside, and nobody knew for how long.
Workers had wages, but nowhere to cash them.
Shopkeepers had goods, but customers had no money.
So the Chamber of Commerce tried something bold.
It issued its own scrip, printed on thin wood.
The wood was run through a newspaper press.
Merchants agreed to take the notes across the counter.
A man could be paid in wood, then buy groceries.
Each note was a promise, passed from hand to hand.
A wooden dollar felt odd, but it still bought bread.
Scrip was a stopgap, but it kept the stores open.
Across America, many towns and companies issued scrip.
Some people kept the notes as souvenirs instead of spending them.
Today, collectors still hunt for those wooden notes.
But Tenino was small. Soon the whole nation lost its banks.
On March sixth, 1933, President Roosevelt closed every bank.
He had been in office for only two days.
More than nine thousand banks had failed since 1930.
Families who lost deposits lost years of careful saving.
Many people had already pulled their cash out and hidden it.
Some kept it in a mattress, or in a coffee can.
The government called the closing a bank holiday.
Nobody standing outside the locked door felt like celebrating.
Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act on March ninth.
Lawmakers passed it in just one day.
On March twelfth, Roosevelt spoke to the nation by radio.
It was the first of his fireside chats.
He explained, in plain words, how banks would reopen.
He told listeners their money was safer in a reopened bank than under the mattress.
Many Americans did bring their money back.
Then came a new idea, insured deposits.
The FDIC opened in January 1934.
It covered up to twenty-five hundred dollars per depositor.
A dollar in a bank finally had a promise behind it.
But most families needed their dollar that very afternoon.
So where did a dollar go the fastest?
Often, to a store with one simple rule.
Frank Woolworth's first lasting five-cent store opened in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in 1879.
By the thirties, five-and-dimes stood on main streets everywhere.
Most things on the counter cost a nickel or a dime.
A dollar could carry home twenty five-cent treasures.
A spool of thread, a toy, a bar of soap.
Woolworth's lunch counters also served cheap meals to shoppers.
A bottle of Coca-Cola cost a nickel.
It had held that price for decades.
A New York subway ride cost a nickel too.
The fare stayed five cents until 1948.
A few nickels could turn an ordinary afternoon into an outing.
Clerks watched closely as children counted their coins.
Pennies mattered. A child's nickel was a serious decision.
But a farm family had a much bigger problem.
Their trouble was not buying things. It was keeping the land.
Crop prices had collapsed, but mortgages still came due.
Banks began to sell farms at foreclosure auctions.
But in some places, neighbors came to every sale.
They stood together, silent, and scared other bidders away.
Then one man bid a few pennies on a plow.
Another bid pennies on a cow, and nobody argued.
The winner handed everything back to the family.
People called it a penny auction.
In 1932, Iowa's Milo Reno founded the Farmers' Holiday Association.
They urged farmers to hold their crops back from market.
Some even blocked roads to stop shipments.
On April twenty-seventh, 1933, anger boiled over in Le Mars, Iowa.
Farmers pulled Judge Charles Bradley from his courtroom.
They demanded that he stop signing foreclosures.
Iowa's governor soon declared martial law there.
One dollar bid, in that fight, could save a home.
And inside those farmhouses, women were thinking about cloth.
Cloth had quietly arrived, inside the feed sack.
Flour, sugar, and chicken feed came in cotton bags.
Thrifty women washed the bags, and then sewed them.
Dresses, shirts, aprons, and curtains came from those bags.
Some women soaked the sacks to wash out the printed brand names.
Then the bag makers noticed what women were doing.
Soon they printed flowers and checks on the cotton.
Mothers asked the store for matching sacks.
A few sacks could become one child's dress.
The fabric came free with the feed.
Thrift was a habit, and nothing was thrown away.
At school, many girls wore the same cheerful prints.
A saved dollar of feed became a dress for school.
If your grandmother saved every scrap of fabric,
she probably learned that in those years.
But some families had no farm, and no flour.
They had sons with no job and nowhere to go.
In spring 1933, Roosevelt created the Civilian Conservation Corps.
The first camp opened in Virginia that April.
At first, it took unmarried men from eighteen to twenty-five.
Young men planted trees, built trails, and fought fires.
They earned thirty dollars a month.
But twenty-five of those dollars went home to their families.
So the boy kept five, and his mother got the rest.
Many boys finally ate three regular meals every day.
They also got clothing, shelter, and medical care.
Some learned to read in camp classes.
Army officers ran the camps, while foresters directed the work.
About three million men served before the program ended in 1942.
They planted roughly three billion trees.
Many of those forests still stand today.
They built park lodges, bridges, and roads we still use.
Every month, a small envelope of money crossed the country.
It paid for coal, shoes, and rent back home.
And on Saturday night, some of it went to the movies.
A movie ticket cost about a quarter.
Even in hard times, people paid for an escape.
Tens of millions of Americans went to the movies every week.
But theater owners still struggled to fill their seats.
So they gave things away. Dishes, mostly.
Collectors now call that glassware Depression glass.
Dish Night gave families a plate or cup each week.
A family could slowly collect a whole set, one night at a time.
Then came Bank Night, a cash drawing.
It spread to thousands of American theaters in the thirties.
Names were drawn from a registry book.
You did not even have to buy a ticket to register.
But you had to be there when your name was called.
So crowds filled the street outside, hoping.
If nobody claimed it, the jackpot grew larger.
Most nights, nobody walked home rich.
Some states later ruled Bank Night an illegal lottery.
But for one evening, a dime felt like hope.
But one game did make a man rich.
Charles Darrow was out of work in Philadelphia.
He sold a handmade board game about buying property.
Atlantic City street names filled his board.
Friends wanted copies, and he made more by hand.
Parker Brothers first turned him down, citing fifty-two design errors.
Then they bought the game in 1935.
But the idea was older than Darrow made it sound.
Lizzie Magie patented The Landlord's Game in 1904.
She meant it to show how landlords gain and tenants lose.
Parker Brothers bought her patent for five hundred dollars.
Monopoly became a best seller in 1935.
Families with empty pockets played with pretend millions.
Rent, houses, hotels, and bankruptcy around the kitchen table.
A child could play banker for an evening.
Darrow earned royalties and became a wealthy man.
Maybe that was the point of the game.
Win the dollar, at least in play.
Now for the last stop, the one I promised.
What was an hour of work actually worth?
Before 1938, there was no national minimum wage.
Some workers earned only pennies for an hour.
On June twenty-fifth, 1938, Roosevelt signed the Fair Labor Standards Act.
It set a minimum wage for many workers.
Twenty-five cents an hour, starting that October.
It also limited hours, with overtime pay beyond forty-four a week.
That limit was lowered to forty hours by 1940.
And it banned most child labor in factories.
Not every job was covered, and many workers were left out.
Farm workers and domestic workers were excluded.
That meant a worker's pay finally had a legal floor.
Still, do the math. Four hours of work earned one dollar.
One dollar meant half a day for some families.
It meant wood, or a movie, or a roof.
So that was the secret of the decade.
A dollar was never just money.
It was time, hope, and a neighbor's help.
If your family ever saved string, jars, or foil,
you may be holding a piece of those years.
